About this document


This document provides the teaching content for Te Ao Haka Years 11–13 of the
New Zealand Curriculum. Equivalent for Te Marautanga o Aotearoa is being
published separately.
Progress and assessment information for Te Ao Haka Years 11–13 is still in
development. Once that is completed, Te Ao Haka Years 11–13 is proposed to be
made by the Minister of Education as a National Curriculum Statement under section
90(1)(a) of the Education and Training Act 2020.
It is proposed that, once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, schools
who offer Te Ao Haka Years 11–13 will be required to start using it in Year 11 from
1 January 2028, in Year 12 from 1 January 2029, and in Year 13 from 1 January
2030.
This document will be replaced with the official version made under the Act and
published in the New Zealand Gazette once that has occurred.

  structure, and apply these insights to enhance their own performance. They make
  connections with other creative forms such as musical composition, theatre,
  choreography, and other Indigenous performance traditions, fostering

Through the study of Te Ao Haka, students are taught to examine relationships
between movement, voice, rhythm, language, performance conventions, artistic
intention, and cultural context. Students connect performance evidence with kaupapa,
whakapapa, tikanga, kōrero tuku iho and meaning within both performance and
written forms.
Te Ao Haka provides students with the knowledge and practices to synthesise
learning from performance traditions, artistic practices, cultural contexts, historical
narratives, contemporary perspectives, and lived experiences. Students examine how
performers and practitioners maintain, adapt, transform, and extend haka and related
performance traditions, and consider relationships between innovation, artistic
expression, whakapapa, tikanga, cultural authority, and cultural integrity.
As students progress through Years 11–13, they are taught to observe, participate,
rehearse, perform, compose, interpret, collaborate, reflect, and refine. Students move
from exploring and applying performance knowledge towards integrating expressive
elements, performance conventions, cultural knowledge, and artistic intention, and
ultimately synthesising these to create authentic, purposeful, and culturally grounded
performances.

 Responsible use of artificial intelligence
 Artificial intelligence (AI) can support learning, research, inquiry, and creative processes, but its use must uphold mana, tikanga, whakapapa, and tino rangatiratanga. AI is not a neutral source of
 knowledge and may reproduce bias, inaccuracies, or understandings inconsistent with mātauranga Māori or the knowledge and values of whānau, hapū, and iwi. Māori knowledge, cultural practices,
 narratives, language, and intellectual and cultural property must be protected from inappropriate collection, use, interpretation, or reproduction.
 Responsible use of AI requires students and teachers to exercise critical judgement and discernment, considering where knowledge comes from, whose perspectives are represented, and whose
 knowledge may be absent or misrepresented. AI should support, not replace, students’ thinking, learning, creativity, relationships, and decision-making. Where Māori knowledge is used, appropriate
 permissions, relationships, attribution, and tikanga must be respected. AI-generated information should be transparently identified and verified against trusted and appropriate sources, including
 mātauranga Māori and the knowledge of whānau, hapū, and iwi.
